Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Title

Staying safe: passwords, scams and personal data

Protect your accounts and other people's data: strong passwords, 2-step verification, spotting scams, and the law.

Next Generation Genius · Year 1 · Foundation

Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Goals

By the end of today

  • Make a strong passphrase and turn on 2-step verification
  • Spot a phishing message
  • Say what personal data is and what Nigeria's data law protects
Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Idea 1

Understand it

Passwords: long beats clever. Three or four random words — plum-river-kettle-sunday — are strong and memorable. Use a different one for every account, especially email (it can reset all the others). A password manager remembers them.

2-step verification (2FA): a code from your phone as well as the password. A stolen password alone then opens nothing.

Phishing messages try to make you click, pay or log in. Warning signs: urgency ("within 24 hours"), a prize you did not enter, a sender address that is nearly right, a link that goes somewhere odd, a request for a code or password. No real bank or school asks for your password or OTP.

Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Idea 2

Understand it

Updates fix security holes: install them.

Personal data — names, phone numbers, photos, addresses, marks — belongs to the person it describes. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 says: ask first, collect only what you need, keep it safe, share it with nobody who should not have it.

Strong passwords and 2FA

Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Key words

Key words

Passphrase
a password made of several random words
2-step verification
a second check, usually a code on your phone
Phishing
a message pretending to be someone trusted to steal details

Data Appreciation · Week 10 · Assessment

How you will be assessed

  • A message says your bank account will close today unless you send the code you just received. What should you do?
  • Show 2-step verification turned on for one account (yours or, with permission, a family one), and explain what it protects against.
  • Which piece of personal data about you would you least want shared, and why? (Private to your instructor.)

Your work is marked against the rubric, and you may be asked to explain your choices. Show your own thinking.
